chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Zakariyya ibn Shayban narrated to us in Sha'ban in the year three and seventy of the two hundred, saying: Ali ibn Sayf ibn 'Umayra narrated to us, from his father, from Humran ibn A'yun, that he said:

I described to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) a man who believes in the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) and exempts himself from his enemy, and believes in all that he says, except that he says: 'They have disagreed among themselves, and they are the leading Imams, and I do not know which of them is the Imam. And if they agree upon one man, we will submit to his word, and I have known that the matter is among them - may Allah have mercy on them all.'
He (Abu Abdillah) said: 'If this man dies, he dies a death of ignorance (Jahiliyyah).'

And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy - devils of mankind and jinn, inspiring to one another decorative speech in delusion. And if your Lord had willed, they would not have done it, so leave them and that which they invent.

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Ali ibn Abi Talib)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on doubting the identity of the Imams according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) critiques the 'waiting for consensus' (intizar) approach, declaring it a 'death of ignorance' because it implies uncertainty in the divinely appointed Imamate rather than firm belief in the specific Twelve. This narration underscores the Shia doctrine of explicit designation (nass), where doubt in the identity of the Imam equates to a return to pre-Islamic ignorance. The concluding verse highlights how this doubt is fueled by the 'deceptive speech' of Shayatin, mirroring the confusion between truth and falsehood.
